paragraphs: This paper studies prediction when test inputs arrive sequentially and their distribution keeps changing. It assumes covariate shift: the frequency of different inputs can change, but the relationship between an input and its output stays the same. The objective is to adapt the predictor so that its accumulated prediction risk remains low over time.

The starting point is importance weighting, which adjusts how much training examples contribute according to their relevance to the current test distribution. The authors show that this approach works effectively when the changing ratios between test and training input densities can be estimated accurately. The difficulty is that each time step supplies too little data for existing estimation methods.

Their online estimator addresses this scarcity by reusing historical information appropriately. A dynamic regret bound describes its ability to track changing conditions and supports an excess prediction risk guarantee. Experiments also support the approach. The contribution connects continual distribution estimation to prediction quality under the stated unchanged input-output relationship.
neurips-2023-adapting-to-continuous-cova.tldr: An online density-ratio estimator reuses historical data to help predictors adapt to continuously changing input distributions.

paragraphs: AdaptSSR addresses how to learn useful user representations when labeled examples are scarce. Existing approaches pretrain on behavior sequences by making augmented versions of the same sequence similar in representation space. That assumes both versions retain the same interests. Diverse interests and noisy behavior can break this assumption, making enforced agreement harmful to later tasks.

The proposed method instead learns relative similarity rankings. Its multiple pairwise ranking loss compares implicitly augmented views, explicitly augmented views, and views belonging to other users. This gives the model a way to distinguish users without requiring every augmented pair to express identical characteristics. Hard negative sampling within a training batch supplies challenging comparisons.

AdaptSSR also adjusts its ranking constraints for individual samples. An adaptive fusion mechanism uses the estimated similarity between augmented views to account for how differently augmentation affects different behavior sequences. Experiments on public and industrial datasets across six downstream tasks support its effectiveness. The central contribution is a pretraining objective that accommodates imperfect preservation of user interests during augmentation.
neurips-2023-adaptssr-pre-training-user-.tldr: AdaptSSR learns user representations through adaptive similarity rankings that accommodate noisy or semantically altered augmentations.

paragraphs: In linear bandits, a learner must choose actions while learning from limited feedback. Selecting among several candidate models introduces another exploration problem: the learner must also decide which model to trust. Treating models as competing experts is a natural strategy, but existing approaches have regret that grows polynomially with the number of models.

The paper introduces ALEXP, which emulates full-information feedback for the online learner. This means constructing feedback that supports comparisons across models despite the limited observations available from bandit interaction. The construction manages a bias-variance trade-off and improves the regret dependence on the number of models from polynomial to logarithmic.

ALEXP also provides anytime guarantees: it does not need to know the eventual number of rounds and requires no initial phase devoted exclusively to exploration. Its analysis uses a new time-uniform treatment of the Lasso, linking model selection in online learning with high-dimensional statistics. The improvement concerns dependence on model count, making that aspect of the guarantee substantially more favorable as the candidate collection grows.
neurips-2023-anytime-model-selection-in-.tldr: ALEXP achieves logarithmic regret dependence on the number of candidate linear-bandit models without requiring a known time horizon.

paragraphs: A vision backbone is the feature extractor on which a larger computer vision system is built. With many architectures, pretraining objectives, and training datasets available, choosing one has become difficult. Battle of the Backbones addresses this practical problem through a broad comparison of pretrained models across several kinds of vision tasks.

The benchmark includes vision-language models, self-supervised models, and the Stable Diffusion backbone. It examines tasks including classification, object detection, and generalization beyond the training distribution, using more than 1,500 training runs. Across the models considered, convolutional networks trained with supervision on large datasets perform best on most tasks.

The comparison also separates that overall finding from more controlled comparisons. When architecture and pretraining dataset size are comparable, self-supervised backbones are highly competitive. This suggests that architecture and data scale deserve attention alongside the learning objective. The authors consequently point toward self-supervised pretraining with stronger architectures and larger datasets, and release results and evaluation code so additional backbones can be assessed.
neurips-2023-battle-of-the-backbones-a-l.tldr: A broad vision benchmark finds supervised convolutional backbones strongest on most tested tasks, with self-supervised models competitive in matched comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates how Bayesian deep learning methods behave when deployment data differ from training data. It examines both predictive performance and calibration, meaning how well reported confidence matches actual correctness. The evaluation uses classification and regression tasks from WILDS and covers large convolutional and transformer architectures.

The authors also investigate a signed calibration error that distinguishes overconfidence from underconfidence. This adds information that a calibration magnitude alone can hide. Their study includes fine-tuning large pretrained models, where training from scratch is prohibitively expensive, and extends posterior approximations focused on a single mode by combining them in ensembles.

Ensembling these approximations generally improves generalization and calibration substantially, but the findings are not uniform across settings. The authors identify an ensemble failure mode when fine-tuning large transformer language models. There, variational approaches such as last-layer Bayes By Backprop achieve substantially better accuracy, while methods such as SWAG provide the best calibration. The results make the training setting and the distinction between accuracy and confidence quality central to method selection.
neurips-2023-beyond-deep-ensembles-a-lar.tldr: A large evaluation finds that Bayesian ensembles generally improve performance under distribution shift, with an important exception in language-model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Beam Tree Recursive Neural Networks build representations through learned tree structures. Earlier work showed strong ability to generalize to longer inputs on ListOps, but the model could still require excessive memory. This paper identifies the coupling between the function that scores choices and the recursive cell that builds representations as its main memory bottleneck.

The authors propose ways to remove that bottleneck and simplify memory use. Their strategies reduce memory consumption by a factor of 10–16, establish a new best result on ListOps, and maintain similar performance on other tasks. These results suggest that restructuring the computation can improve practical efficiency without sacrificing the capabilities measured in the study.

A second contribution changes what the network returns. Instead of producing one vector for an entire sentence, it uses representations from the learned tree nodes to produce a contextual representation for every token. This makes the model easier to stack or connect with Transformers and Structured State Space models, expanding its role from a sentence encoder to a reusable sequence-processing component.
neurips-2023-efficient-beam-tree-recursi.tldr: Separating scoring from recursive computation cuts BT-RvNN memory use by 10–16 times and enables contextual outputs for individual tokens.

paragraphs: The Whittle index policy offers a heuristic for the computationally difficult restless multi-armed bandit problem, but computing its indices is itself challenging. This paper presents Neural-Q-Whittle, which combines index learning with Q-learning and neural network function approximation. Its main focus is understanding how quickly this coupled learning procedure converges.

The algorithm operates on two timescales. Q-function estimates change on the faster timescale, while Whittle indices update more slowly. The analysis considers observations generated by a Markov chain and a Q-function represented by a ReLU neural network. These features require accounting for dependent data, interacting updates, and nonlinear approximation within the same argument.

The authors use a Lyapunov drift approach to track the evolution of the two coupled parameter sets and characterize the neural approximation error. Together, these steps yield an O(1/k^(2/3)) convergence rate after k iterations in the analyzed setting. The contribution supplies a finite-iteration characterization, making the learning dynamics more explicit than an eventual-convergence statement alone.
neurips-2023-finite-time-analysis-of-whi.tldr: Neural-Q-Whittle receives a finite-time convergence analysis for coupled neural Q-learning and Whittle-index updates with Markov-chain data.

paragraphs: FourierHandFlow represents the three-dimensional shape of a human hand continuously through time using RGB video. The paper targets weaknesses in existing implicit shape representations: they can miss correspondences between articulated shapes or produce jittery temporal changes. Its approach combines a spatial occupancy field with flows that describe how queries move as the hand changes.

Each query flow is represented by a fixed collection of Fourier coefficients, providing smooth, continuous temporal dynamics. The representation separates two kinds of change. Pose flow captures motion associated with articulation through implicit linear blend skinning, while shape flow captures displacement at individual query locations. This structure brings articulation information into the temporal representation.

Experiments report state-of-the-art video-based 4D reconstruction results and greater computational efficiency than the existing 3D and 4D implicit representations considered. The authors also demonstrate motion interpolation, extrapolation, and texture transfer using learned shape correspondences. These applications show how a continuous representation can support relationships across time as well as reconstruction of individual hand shapes.
neurips-2023-fourierhandflow-neural-4d-h.tldr: FourierHandFlow combines articulation-aware Fourier flows with an occupancy field to reconstruct smoothly changing hand shapes from RGB video.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can reconstruct image details during deblurring, but generating a clean image through many denoising iterations is computationally expensive. Their generated results can also differ from the target in ways that hurt distortion-based measurements. HI-Diff addresses both issues by assigning diffusion and direct image restoration different roles.

The diffusion model operates in a highly compressed latent space and generates a prior feature to guide restoration. A regression-based model performs the actual deblurring, supporting better distortion accuracy. Working in the compact latent space makes the diffusion component efficient, while its output still contributes information to the reconstruction process.

A hierarchical integration module inserts this prior into the regression model at multiple scales. The design aims to improve generalization across complicated blur conditions by making the generated information available throughout the restoration hierarchy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world blur datasets report performance above state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a combined design that uses diffusion-derived guidance alongside regression-based reconstruction.
neurips-2023-hierarchical-integration-di.tldr: HI-Diff uses compact latent diffusion to guide a multiscale regression model for efficient, accurate image deblurring.

paragraphs: Holistic transfer asks how to adapt a pretrained classifier to a new domain when the available target data contain only some of its classes. The adapted model must still recognize every class from the source data. This reflects a practical situation in which end users cannot collect target examples for the full classification task.

The authors construct benchmarks and investigate the resulting tension. Adapting to the new domain matters for performance, but maintaining accuracy on classes absent from the adaptation data is difficult. Evaluating only the classes represented during adaptation would therefore miss an essential part of the intended behavior.

The paper identifies two directions for addressing the problem: separating domain-related gradients from classification-related gradients, and preserving relationships among classes. It presents several solutions that maintain accuracy for missing classes while improving overall performance in the experiments. These methods establish baselines for adaptation that accounts for the complete original label space, including classes for which the user supplies no target examples.
neurips-2023-holistic-transfer-towards-n.tldr: Holistic transfer adapts classifiers using partial target-class data while seeking to preserve accuracy on the classes missing from adaptation.

paragraphs: LAMP investigates whether a language model can help predict future events by reasoning about possible explanations for them. It combines this reasoning with an event sequence model that already proposes future events based on past observations. The language model contributes abductive reasoning: suggesting causes that could make a proposed event plausible.

A few expert-annotated demonstrations guide the language model in producing those possible causes. A search module then retrieves earlier events matching the suggestions. Finally, a learned scoring function examines whether those retrieved events could cause the proposed future event. The framework thus connects a proposed prediction to potentially relevant evidence in the observed history.

Experiments on several challenging real-world datasets show that LAMP can substantially outperform state-of-the-art event sequence models. The result supports using language-model reasoning as an additional component in event prediction. Its cause suggestions are intermediate hypotheses assessed through retrieval and scoring; the described evaluation establishes improved prediction performance rather than verified causal explanations for every event.
neurips-2023-language-models-can-improve.tldr: LAMP improves event prediction by using language-model-generated possible causes to retrieve and score relevant historical events.

paragraphs: MultiMon aims to discover categories of multimodal model failures before deployment. Its target is a systematic failure: a recurring pattern that can be described in ordinary language and illustrated by many inputs. Such patterns give evaluators a way to examine broader weaknesses instead of treating every erroneous result as an isolated case.

The system starts by collecting examples of erroneous agreement, where inputs produce the same output even though they should differ. It prompts a language model to identify shared patterns and describe them. Applied to CLIP's text encoder, MultiMon finds 14 systematic failures, each supported by hundreds of distinct inputs, including failure to distinguish quantities expressed in text.

The authors show that these inputs also produce failures in multimodal systems including Midjourney 5.1, DALL-E, and VideoFusion. MultiMon can steer discovery toward particular applications, such as self-driving cars. The work demonstrates a route toward automated evaluation that searches for overlooked failure categories and makes them understandable through descriptions and concrete examples.
neurips-2023-mass-producing-failures-of-.tldr: MultiMon uses a language model to turn examples of erroneous agreement into reusable descriptions of systematic multimodal failures.

paragraphs: Langevin sampling uses information about a target distribution to guide movement through its parameter space. This paper studies preconditioning, which changes the scale and direction of those movements. The authors define an optimal choice through a specific objective: maximizing the expected squared distance traveled by the Langevin diffusion.

Solving that optimization yields an inverse Fisher information covariance matrix. The matrix being inverted is obtained by averaging outer products of gradients of the log target distribution under the target itself. This gives an analytic connection between the target's gradient structure and the preconditioner preferred by the chosen movement criterion.

The authors apply the result to the Metropolis adjusted Langevin algorithm and construct an efficient adaptive sampler that learns its preconditioner from gradients accumulated during sampling. Experiments show strong robustness in high dimensions and substantial improvements over the compared methods, including another adaptive MALA scheme and position-dependent Riemannian manifold MALA. The optimality statement concerns the specified expected-movement objective, while the broader performance advantage is demonstrated empirically.
neurips-2023-optimal-preconditioning-and.tldr: An analytically derived inverse-Fisher preconditioner enables an adaptive Langevin sampler that learns effective movement geometry from past gradients.

paragraphs: Conditional Neural Processes are meta-learning models that combine efficient inference with uncertainty estimates. Many tasks they address contain equivariances: transformations of the inputs that should produce corresponding transformations in predictions. Translation is one example. Incorporating such structure lets a model account for relationships already inherent in the task.

Existing efforts to build equivariances into these models have difficulty scaling beyond two input dimensions. The paper proposes Relational Conditional Neural Processes as a way to incorporate equivariances into any neural process model. Its central contribution is extending the practical reach of equivariant neural processes to higher-dimensional inputs.

The authors evaluate RCNPs across a broad collection of tasks that naturally possess these transformation relationships and report competitive performance. The motivation includes settings such as spatiotemporal modeling, Bayesian optimization, and continuous control. The findings support RCNPs as a practical approach for incorporating task structure while working within the neural process framework, with the dimensional scalability issue serving as the specific obstacle the method addresses.
neurips-2023-practical-equivariances-via.tldr: Relational Conditional Neural Processes make equivariance practical for neural process models with higher-dimensional inputs.

paragraphs: This paper examines class imbalance in graph neural networks used to classify nodes. When classes are represented unevenly, learning must cope with differences in the available evidence for each class. The authors approach this problem through bias-variance decomposition, developing a theoretical framework that closely connects imbalance with model variance.

That connection motivates a concrete training method. The approach uses graph augmentation to estimate variance, then introduces a regularization term intended to reduce the effects of imbalance. Variance therefore serves both as an explanatory concept and as a quantity used to shape learning, connecting the theoretical perspective to the proposed intervention.

The evaluation covers multiple benchmarks, including naturally imbalanced datasets and class-imbalanced datasets using public splits. The authors report performance above state-of-the-art methods across the tested imbalance scenarios. These findings support treating variance as a useful target when designing graph classifiers for uneven class distributions. The contribution combines a perspective on why imbalance matters with an augmentation-based way to estimate and address its effects.
neurips-2023-rethinking-semi-supervised-.tldr: A bias-variance view of imbalanced graph classification motivates augmentation-based variance estimation and a regularizer that improves benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Masked image modeling pretrains vision models by reconstructing hidden image content. Existing methods commonly discard the decoder before downstream use, creating a mismatch between pretraining and fine-tuning representations that can hurt performance. RevColV2 addresses this by retaining the entire autoencoder during both stages.

The architecture contains bottom-up and top-down columns that exchange information reversibly. As information passes through them, low-level details and semantic content become progressively disentangled. The design preserves these distinct kinds of information at the network's end during pretraining, supporting downstream use of the complete architecture.

Experiments suggest that this separation yields competitive classification, segmentation, and detection performance. After intermediate ImageNet-22K fine-tuning, RevColV2-L reaches 88.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and 58.6 mIoU on ADE20K. With an additional teacher and large-scale dataset, it reaches 62.1 box AP on COCO and 60.4 mIoU on ADE20K. Those results come from different training conditions and illustrate the architecture's performance across several vision tasks.
neurips-2023-revcolv2-exploring-disentan.tldr: RevColV2 retains the full autoencoder through fine-tuning and separates low-level from semantic information for competitive downstream vision performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the choice of optimization algorithm affects the solution learned by a two-layer diagonal linear network. In overparameterized regression, optimization can favor particular solutions even without an explicit regularization penalty. The authors investigate how this implicit regularization changes with stochastic updates and large learning steps.

They prove convergence for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent with macroscopic step sizes in the setting studied. They also characterize the resulting solutions through an implicit regularization problem. This characterization makes it possible to examine how step size and stochasticity influence the kind of regression solution recovered.

The findings distinguish the two algorithms. Large steps consistently benefit stochastic gradient descent on sparse regression problems in this setting, while they can make ordinary gradient descent worse at recovering sparse solutions. These effects intensify in a narrow range just below the divergence threshold, called the edge-of-stability regime. Experiments support the theoretical findings, showing that the consequences of larger steps depend on the update procedure within the analyzed network class.
neurips-2023-s-gd-over-diagonal-linear-n.tldr: For diagonal linear networks, large steps favor sparse recovery with SGD but can hinder it with gradient descent, especially near instability.

paragraphs: Safe exploration asks how a reinforcement learning agent can improve its behavior while respecting safety constraints during learning. This paper introduces a generalized formulation that unifies common versions of the problem. It then proposes MASE, a meta-algorithm combining an unconstrained reinforcement learning method with a mechanism for quantifying uncertainty.

MASE uses that uncertainty information to maintain safety in the current episode and penalize unsafe exploration before a violation occurs. These penalties discourage similar exploration in later episodes. Under appropriate assumptions, the method supports policy optimization while guaranteeing a high probability that no safety constraint is violated.

The paper develops two variants. One uses generalized linear models and has theoretical safety and near-optimality guarantees. The other combines a Gaussian process for safety with deep reinforcement learning for reward maximization. On grid-world and Safety Gym benchmarks, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms without observed safety violations, including during training. These empirical outcomes complement the conditional, high-probability theoretical guarantee.
neurips-2023-safe-exploration-in-reinfor.tldr: MASE combines reinforcement learning with uncertainty estimates to support safe exploration with high-probability guarantees under appropriate assumptions.

paragraphs: Machine learning methods for partial differential equations often rely on simulated training data prepared for a particular setting. This paper investigates learning more general representations from heterogeneous data. The motivation is to make useful information available across varied sources, including the broader challenge of observations from dynamical systems that may be messy or incomplete.

The authors apply joint embedding methods for self-supervised learning, bringing a representation-learning framework used successfully in computer vision into the PDE setting. The aim is to learn representations that support multiple uses, instead of making the training objective specific to just one solver task. Lie symmetries provide the paper's stated organizing theme.

The learned representation outperforms baseline approaches on invariant tasks, including estimating PDE coefficients, and improves the time-stepping performance of neural solvers. These findings connect representation quality to both identifying properties of equations and advancing their solutions through time. The authors present the methodology as a possible step toward general-purpose PDE foundation models, leaving that broader goal as a future prospect.
neurips-2023-self-supervised-learning-wi.tldr: Self-supervised joint embeddings learn PDE representations from heterogeneous data that improve coefficient estimation and neural-solver time stepping.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from multiple camera views is economically attractive compared with LiDAR, but images lack equally precise spatial cues. STXD improves image-based detectors through a teacher-student setup: a stronger LiDAR model supplies knowledge during training. The paper argues that simply minimizing global differences between their features can leave useful information poorly transferred.

Its structural component regularizes correlations between teacher and student features while increasing their similarity, reducing redundancy among student feature components. Its temporal component represents relationships across frames using similarity maps. This gives the student supervision about how features relate over time, alongside information about their structure within the representations.

STXD also transfers knowledge at the output level through response distillation. Together, these components address feature structure, temporal relationships, and final predictions. Experiments on the nuScenes test set report improvements of 2.8%–4.5% in NDS and mAP for the underlying student detectors. The findings support a richer transfer objective for improving multi-view image-based 3D detection.
neurips-2023-stxd-structural-and-tempora.tldr: STXD improves camera-based 3D detection by transferring structural, temporal, and output-level knowledge from a LiDAR teacher.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks predict interactions in systems whose connections change over time. Understanding these predictions requires identifying which patterns in the interaction history matter to the model. TempME focuses on temporal motifs: recurring arrangements of interactions that can provide a meaningful unit for explaining a prediction.

The method uses the information bottleneck principle to select motifs strongly related to the interaction being predicted while limiting the amount of information retained. This balances relevance with concise explanations. Instead of returning an unnecessarily large collection of events, it aims to identify a sparse set of patterns that captures the model's key predictive evidence.

The authors find that events selected by TempME are more closely connected in space and time than those selected by existing approaches. Across six real-world datasets, they report explanation accuracy improvements of up to 8.21% and increases of up to 22.96% in prediction Average Precision for current temporal graph models. These are reported maximum gains, supporting both the explanatory usefulness and potential predictive value of motif discovery.
neurips-2023-tempme-towards-the-explaina.tldr: TempME explains temporal graph predictions by selecting compact, relevant recurring interaction patterns.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning becomes challenging when participating clients use different network architectures. The paper addresses this model heterogeneity with pFedHR, a framework based on heterogeneous model reassembly. Its objective is to produce models suited to individual clients while accommodating differences in the structures they bring to the collaboration.

The framework formulates personalization as a model-matching optimization problem on the server. It automatically generates informative, varied candidate models and updates those candidates dynamically, requiring little human intervention. This makes the construction and selection of personalized architectures part of the learning framework rather than a choice that must remain fixed throughout the process.

Experiments on three datasets show pFedHR outperforming baselines under both IID and non-IID conditions, covering different degrees of similarity among clients' data distributions. The method also reduces, to an extent, the adverse effects of public data whose distribution differs from client data. The reported benefits therefore concern both architectural diversity and resilience to the public-data mismatch involved in the evaluated personalization process.
neurips-2023-towards-personalized-federa.tldr: pFedHR dynamically reassembles heterogeneous models into personalized candidates and partially reduces the effects of mismatched public data.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover a hidden signal from indirect, usually noisy observations. Bayesian methods use prior distributions to regularize this recovery and express remaining uncertainty, but sampling-based computation can be expensive. This paper examines the theoretical behavior of a more computationally practical alternative: variational inference with Gaussian process priors.

The analysis focuses on inducing-variable variational methods for linear inverse problems. It covers both mildly and severely ill-posed settings, where recovering the underlying signal can be increasingly difficult. The authors derive posterior contraction rates, describing how quickly the approximate posterior concentrates around the true signal as information accumulates.

They show that correctly tuned procedures can attain the minimax estimation rate, the benchmark for best achievable worst-case estimation accuracy in the setting. This is a conditional result about suitable tuning, rather than a guarantee for every variational approximation. Examples include inverse problems involving the heat equation, the Volterra operator, and the Radon transform, with inducing variables based on population or empirical spectral features.
neurips-2023-variational-gaussian-proces.tldr: Properly tuned inducing-variable Gaussian process approximations can achieve minimax estimation rates for linear inverse problems.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize inputs that differ from the data a model is intended to handle. A major difficulty is that models can remain overconfident on such inputs. One existing method, ReAct, clips large internal activations to make familiar and unfamiliar inputs easier to distinguish.

This paper asks whether clipping only the largest activations is the best operation. Using a variational analysis, the authors derive an optimal operation and find support for suppressing unusually low and unusually high activations while strengthening intermediate ones. The analysis motivates treating the activation range more broadly when constructing a detector.

Variational Rectified Activation, or VRA, implements these suppression and amplification behaviors through piecewise functions. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show it outperforming existing post-hoc strategies, and the method works with different scoring functions and network architectures. Its contribution connects a theoretically motivated activation transformation with a practical detection technique, broadening the intervention beyond the high-activation truncation used by ReAct.
neurips-2023-vra-variational-rectified-a.tldr: VRA improves out-of-distribution detection by suppressing extreme activations and amplifying intermediate ones using piecewise transformations.

paragraphs: YouTube-ASL addresses a data bottleneck in machine learning for sign languages. The corpus pairs American Sign Language videos from YouTube with accompanying English captions. Its open-domain scope supplies material for learning ASL-to-English translation from a large collection of videos and signers.

The dataset contains approximately 1,000 hours of video and more than 2,500 unique signers. Compared with the largest prior ASL dataset described in the paper, it provides roughly three times as much video and ten times as many signers. Those two dimensions distinguish the contribution: it expands both the quantity of material and the number of people represented.

The authors train baseline translation models on YouTube-ASL and evaluate them on How2Sign. After fine-tuning, they report a new state-of-the-art result of 12.397 BLEU. They also report the first nontrivial zero-shot results on that evaluation. Together, these outcomes demonstrate the corpus's usefulness for training translation models and transferring them to a separate evaluation dataset, with fine-tuned and zero-shot performance representing distinct conditions.
neurips-2023-youtube-asl-a-large-scale-o.tldr: YouTube-ASL expands paired ASL-English training data and enables improved fine-tuned and nontrivial zero-shot translation results on How2Sign.
